## Statement

Assume Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. Let $E\subseteq\mathbb Z^d$ be countable and let a finite-channel system be as in [[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]]. For an initial state $x_0\in E$, construct its minimal reaction process recursively: at state $x$, wait an exponential time with parameter $\lambda(x)$, choose channel $j$ with probability $a_j(x)/\lambda(x)$, and move to $x+\nu_j$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, remain at $x$ forever. Use an independent stream of these exponential and uniform random inputs, whose countable product law exists by Countable Choice and Dependent Choice.

For $V:E\to[1,\infty)$, call $V$ **proper** when $\{x:V(x)\le n\}$ is finite for every integer $n\ge1$. For this possibly unbounded $V$, define the finite local expression
$$(QV)(x):=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)\bigl(V(x+\nu_j)-V(x)\bigr);$$
this does not assert that $V$ belongs to the bounded-function domain of the generator in [F1]. Suppose $QV\le cV$ for a constant $c\ge0$. Define $T_m$ as the time of the $m$th reaction event, with $T_m=\infty$ if fewer than $m$ events occur. Then the explosion time $\tau_\infty:=\lim_{m\to\infty}T_m$ satisfies $\mathbb P_{x_0}(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. No full Axiom of Choice is used.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Countable Choice, Dependent Choice, a countable reaction network, a deterministic initial state $x_0$, the independent random input stream, a proper $V\ge1$, and $QV\le cV$.

[F1] A reaction system has finitely many channels, finite total rate at each state, admissible poststates, and generator operator $Qf(x)=\sum_{j:a_j(x)>0}a_j(x)(f(x+\nu_j)-f(x))$ for bounded $f$; for the stated $V$, the theorem uses that same finite sum as a local expression. ([[def-reaction-network-propensity-system-and-generator]])

[F2] Unit exponential waiting times have density $e^{-t}$ on $t>0$, survival $e^{-t}$, and rescaling by $\lambda>0$ gives the exponential holding law of parameter $\lambda$. ([[thm-exponential-and-weibull-survival-laws]])

[F3] Under Countable Choice and Dependent Choice, a countable sequence of probability spaces has a probability product with the required finite-coordinate product marginals; normalized Lebesgue measure supplies the uniform coordinates, and the coordinate laws are random-element laws. ([[thm-countable-product-of-probability-spaces]], [[def-independent-random-elements]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]], [[thm-lebesgue-measure-of-a-box-of-every-kind]])

[F4] Expectation is integration against the probability measure, is linear on integrable variables, and preserves almost-sure order. ([[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]], [[cor-expectation-linearity-monotonicity-and-modulus-bound]])

[A1] Countable Choice is used only in the stated exponential and probability-product existence interfaces. ([[def-countable-choice]])

[A2] Dependent Choice is used only in the countable-product probability-space construction. ([[def-dependent-choice]])

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Fix $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$ and set $K_n=\{x\in E:V(x)\le n\}$. This is finite by properness. The set $D_n=\{x+\nu_j:x\in K_n,\ a_j(x)>0,\ 1\le j\le R\}\setminus K_n$ of one-reaction exit states is finite, and $F_n=K_n\cup D_n$ is finite. The rate bound $M_n:=\max_{x\in K_n}\lambda(x)$ is therefore finite. For fixed ordered channel labels $j_1,\ldots,j_m$, the density of event times $0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$ before the first exit is the product of the successive channel rates and exponential no-event factors. Summing over channel labels bounds this density by $M_n^m$, since at each event the sum of active channel rates is at most $M_n$. The ordered simplex has volume $T^m/m!$, so the probability of at least $m$ events before exit by $T$ is at most $(M_nT)^m/m!$, which tends to zero. Thus infinitely many jumps cannot occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$. [A1, A2, F1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 Stop the process at $\tau_n:=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t\notin K_n\}$. The stopped path takes values in the finite set $F_n$ and is frozen after exit. Let $C_n=\max_{y\in F_n}V(y)$. Conditional on the reaction history through time $s$, partition on the finite vector of last-used stream indices; on each part [F3] gives independence of all unused coordinates. If $s$ falls within a holding interval, the residual exponential wait has the same law because $e^{-\lambda(w+u)}/e^{-\lambda w}=e^{-\lambda u}$. Thus for $x=X_s\in K_n$, the density of one channel-$j$ event at elapsed time $u$ and no earlier event is $a_j(x)e^{-\lambda(x)u}$. The probability of at least two events within $h$ is at most $(M_nh)^2/2$ by integrating the summed first-two-event density, bounded by $M_n^2$, over the ordered two-time simplex. Since $V\le C_n$ on $F_n$, the first-event term differs from $h(QV)(x)$ by at most $C_nM_n^2h^2/2$, using $|1-e^{-z}|\le z$ for $z\ge0$; the multiple-event remainder is bounded by $2C_n(M_nh)^2/2$. Thus, uniformly over $x\in K_n$, $\mathbb E[V(X_{(s+h)\wedge\tau_n})-V(X_{s\wedge\tau_n})\mid\mathcal F_s]=h\,1_{\{s<\tau_n\}}(QV)(X_s)+O(h^2).$ Summing this identity on a uniform partition of $[0,t]$ and letting the mesh tend to zero gives $\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]=V(x_0)+\mathbb E\int_0^{t\wedge\tau_n}(QV)(X_s)\,ds.$ The error sum is $O(th)$; the Riemann sums converge because the stopped path has finitely many jumps by step 1.1 and $QV$ is bounded on $K_n$. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, given, algebra]

3.1 Set $g_n(t)=\mathbb E[V(X_{t\wedge\tau_n})]$. From step 2.1, $QV\le cV$, and $V\ge1$, we obtain $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)+c\int_0^t g_n(s)\,ds.$ Here $g_n$ is bounded on each finite interval because $X_{t\wedge\tau_n}\in F_n$. Iterating the integral inequality $m$ times bounds it by $V(x_0)\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(ct)^k/k!+C_n(ct)^m/m!$; the last term tends to zero and the sum tends to $V(x_0)e^{ct}$. Hence $g_n(t)\le V(x_0)e^{ct}$. [F4, step 2.1, given, algebra]

4.1 On $\{\tau_n\le T\}$ the exit state satisfies $V(X_{\tau_n})>n$, so $n\,\mathbb P(\tau_n\le T)\le g_n(T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}$. [F4, step 3.1, given, algebra]

5.1 Fix any finite $T>0$. If $\tau_\infty\le T$ but $\tau_n>T$ for some integer $n\ge\max\{1,V(x_0)\}$, infinitely many events occur in finite time while the process remains in $K_n$, an event of probability zero by step 1.1. A countable union over such $n$ is still null, so outside it explosion by $T$ forces $\tau_n\le T$ for every sufficiently large integer $n$. Step 4.1 gives $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty\le T)\le V(x_0)e^{cT}/n$ for arbitrarily large $n$, hence this probability is zero. Taking integer $T\ge1$ proves $\mathbb P(\tau_\infty=\infty)=1$. The argument uses Countable Choice and Dependent Choice only as declared in [A1] and [A2]; it uses no Axiom of Choice. [A1, A2, F3, step 1.1, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]),
so that $r^0 = 1$ for every $r$, including $r = 0$.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and
   $$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} r^{k} \;=\; \frac{1}{1-r} .$$
2. If $|r| \ge 1$ then $\sum r^k$ diverges.

The series starts at $k = 0$ and its first term is $r^0 = 1$; in particular
$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} 2^{-k} = 2$, while the series starting at $k = 1$ sums to
$1$. Which starting index is meant has to be said, and it is said here.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A real number $r$, the integer powers $r^k$ ([[def-integer-power]]), and the partial sums $s_n = \sum_{k<n} r^k$ of $\sum r^k$ ([[def-series]], [[def-finite-sum]]).

[L1] Factorisation of a difference of powers: for $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ and natural $n \ge 1$, $b^n - a^n = (b-a)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} a^k b^{\,n-1-k}$ ([[lem-power-difference-factorisation]]).

[L2] For $|r| < 1$ the sequence $(r^k)$ is null, that is $r^k \to 0$ ([[lem-geometric-sequence-null]]).

[L3] Algebra of limits: sums, differences and quotients of convergent sequences converge to the corresponding combination, the quotient rule requiring a nonzero limit and nonzero denominators ([[thm-algebra-of-limits]], [[def-real-limit]]).

[L4] Absolute value: $|xy| = |x|\,|y|$, $|x| \ge 0$, and $|x| = 0$ exactly when $x = 0$; also $|1| = 1$, since $1 > 0$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]]).

[L5] Powers and order: $a^0 = 1$ for every $a$; if $a \ge 1$ and $n \ge 1$ then $a^n \ge a \ge 1$; and $1^n = 1$ for every $n$ ([[lem-power-monotone]], [[def-integer-power]]).

[L6] The principle of induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]).

[L7] If a series converges then its terms tend to $0$ ([[lem-nth-term-test]]).

[L8] Notation of [[def-finite-sum]]: $\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} x_k$ is $\sum_{k<n} x_k$, and the empty sum $\sum_{k<0} x_k$ is $0$.

## Proof

**Proof technique:** cases.

1.1 Assume $|r| < 1$. [assume-case lt]

1.2 Assume instead $|r| \ge 1$. [assume-case ge]

1.3 For every natural $n \ge 1$, applying [L1] with $b = 1$ and $a = r$ gives $1 - r^n = (1-r)\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} r^k \cdot 1^{\,n-1-k} = (1-r)\,s_n$, using $1^m = 1$ and the notation of [L8]. [L1, L5, L8]

1.4 At $n = 0$ the identity $1 - r^n = (1-r)s_n$ also holds, both sides being $0$ because $r^0 = 1$ and $s_0$ is the empty sum. [L5, L8]

2.1 In the case $|r| < 1$ we have $r \ne 1$, since $|1| = 1$ and $|r| < 1$; hence $1 - r \ne 0$. [step 1.1, L4, algebra]

2.2 In the case $|r| \ge 1$, an induction gives $|r^k| = |r|^k$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$: at $k = 0$ both sides are $1$, and if $|r^k| = |r|^k$ then $|r^{k+1}| = |r^k \cdot r| = |r^k|\,|r| = |r|^k |r| = |r|^{k+1}$. [step 1.2, L4, L5, L6]

2.3 In the case $|r| \ge 1$ we get $|r|^k \ge 1$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$: at $k = 0$ this reads $1 \ge 1$, and for $k \ge 1$ it is the comparison $|r|^k \ge |r| \ge 1$. [step 1.2, L5]

3.1 In the case $|r| < 1$, dividing by $1 - r \ne 0$ gives $s_n = (1 - r^n)/(1-r)$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$. [step 2.1, step 1.3, step 1.4, algebra]

3.2 In the case $|r| \ge 1$, combining the two previous steps gives $|r^k - 0| = |r^k| = |r|^k \ge 1$ for every $k \in \mathbb{N}$. [step 2.2, step 2.3]

4.1 In the case $|r| < 1$ the sequence $(r^n)$ is null, so $1 - r^n \to 1$ and therefore $s_n \to 1/(1-r)$, the denominator being the nonzero constant $1-r$; hence $\sum r^k$ converges with sum $1/(1-r)$, which is claim 1. [step 1.1, step 3.1, step 2.1, L2, L3]

4.2 In the case $|r| \ge 1$ the sequence $(r^k)$ does not converge to $0$, since the rational tolerance $\varepsilon = 1$ admits no index $K$ with $|r^k - 0| < 1$ for all $k \ge K$; so by the term test $\sum r^k$ diverges, which is claim 2. [step 3.2, L7]

5.1 The two cases $|r| < 1$ and $|r| \ge 1$ exhaust the possibilities, since the order on $\mathbb{R}$ is total, so claims 1 and 2 together cover every real $r$. [step 4.1, step 4.2, cases-exhaustive] ∎

## Remarks

- **The divergence half needs no separate treatment of $r = 1$ and $r = -1$.** Both are covered by $|r| \ge 1$, and the single reason is the same in every case: the terms have absolute value at least $1$, so they cannot tend to $0$. For $r = 1$ the partial sums are $s_n = n$ and run to $+\infty$; for $r = -1$ they oscillate between $0$ and $1$. The theorem says only that neither converges, which is all that "diverges" means here ([[def-series]]).

- **Why the identity is proved at $n = 0$ separately.** [[lem-power-difference-factorisation]] requires $n \ge 1$, since its right-hand side is a sum over $k < n$ of a term involving $b^{\,n-1-k}$, and $n-1$ is not a natural number at $n = 0$. The identity is still true at $n = 0$, but by inspection of two empty objects rather than by that lemma, and step 1.4 says so rather than letting the reader assume the citation covers it.

## Statement

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A rational $p\ge 1$, natural numbers $m,n,q$, matrices $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$, and vectors $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

[L1] $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ and on $\mathbb{R}^{m}$: in particular $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$ and $\lVert\lambda y\rVert_p=|\lambda|\lVert y\rVert_p$ ([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

[L2] The induced norm is $\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup\{\lVert Ay\rVert_p:\lVert y\rVert_p\le 1\}$ ([[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]]).

[L3] Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)x=A(Bx)$; it is also unital, so $I_nx=x$ for $n\ge 1$ ([[thm-matrix-multiplication-laws]], [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $x=0$ the compatibility claim reads $0\le \lVert A\rVert_p\cdot 0$, which is true by [L1] and [L2]. [L1, L2, algebra]

1.2 For $x\ne 0$ the vector $\lVert x\rVert_p>0$ by [L1], so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p/\lVert x\rVert_p=\lVert A(x/\lVert x\rVert_p)\rVert_p$ by homogeneity of [L1]. [L1, algebra]

1.3 For claim 2, if $q=0$, then $B\in M_{n\times0}(\mathbb R)$ and $AB\in M_{m\times0}(\mathbb R)$ are empty matrices. Their domains contain only the zero vector, so the unit-ball definition [L2] gives $\lVert B\rVert_p=\lVert AB\rVert_p=0$. Thus $\lVert AB\rVert_p=0=\lVert A\rVert_p\lVert B\rVert_p$, proving claim 2 in this case without a ratio supremum. [L1, L2, L3, algebra]

1.4 For $n\ge 1$ every $x\ne 0$ attains ratio one: by [L3], $\lVert I_nx\rVert_p=\lVert x\rVert_p$, so $\lVert I_nx\rVert_p/\lVert x\rVert_p=1$, and the supremum in [L2] is therefore $1$, which is claim 3 for $n\ge 1$. [L2, L3, algebra]

1.5 At $n=0$ the space $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has only the zero vector, so the definition of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]] assigns $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, which is the stated exceptional value. [L2, algebra]

2.1 The scaled vector $x/\lVert x\rVert_p$ has $p$-norm $1$, so $\lVert A(x/\lVert x\rVert_p)\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p$ by [L2]; combining step 1.2 with this bound gives $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\lVert x\rVert_p$, which with step 1.1 proves claim 1. [step 1.2, L2, algebra]

3.1 For the remaining case $q\ge1$, let $x\in\mathbb R^q$ with $x\ne0$. Associativity of [L3] gives $\lVert(AB)x\rVert_p=\lVert A(Bx)\rVert_p$, and applying claim 1 first to $A$ at the vector $Bx$ and then to $B$ at the vector $x$ gives $\lVert A(Bx)\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\lVert Bx\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\lVert B\rVert_p\lVert x\rVert_p$. [step 2.1, L3, algebra]

4.1 Still assuming $q\ge1$, dividing step 3.1 by the positive number $\lVert x\rVert_p$ and taking the supremum over all nonzero $x$ in the definition of [L2] gives $\lVert AB\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\lVert B\rVert_p$; with step 1.3 this is claim 2. [step 3.1, L1, L2, algebra]

5.1 Claim 1 is step 2.1. Claim 2 follows from step 1.3 when $q=0$ and step 4.1 when $q\ge1$. Claim 3 is steps 1.4 and 1.5. [step 2.1, step 1.3, step 4.1, step 1.4, step 1.5] ∎

## Statement

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\ge 1$ and $n\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, with the induced $1$-norm and the
separately defined induced $\infty$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Maximum column sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_1=\max_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|$.
2. **Maximum row sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Natural numbers $m,n\ge 1$, a matrix $A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, and vectors $x=(x_j)\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

[L1] The $1$-norm and the $\infty$-norm are $\lVert x\rVert_1=\sum_{j<n}|x_j|$ and $\lVert x\rVert_\infty=\max\{|x_j|:j<n\}$ ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]); each is a norm, in particular the triangle inequality and $|x_j|\le\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ hold ([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]).

[L2] The induced norm is the supremum of the ratio over nonzero vectors, and compatibility gives $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le\lVert A\rVert_p\lVert x\rVert_p$ ([[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]], [[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]]).

[L3] The standard basis vector $e_j\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ satisfies $e_j(j)=1$ and $e_j(k)=0$ for $k\ne j$, and finite sums are evaluated pointwise; in particular $(Ae_j)_i=a_{ij}$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Write $C:=\max_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|$; the maximum exists because it is a maximum of the nonempty finite set of column sums of [L1]. [given, L1]

1.2 Expanding the matrix-vector product entrywise and using the triangle inequality and absolute multiplicativity of [L1] gives $\lVert Ax\rVert_1=\sum_{i<m}\bigl|\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}x_j\bigr|\le\sum_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|$. [L1, algebra]

1.3 Write $R:=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$, a maximum of a nonempty finite set of row sums by [L1]. [L1]

2.1 Exchanging the finite double sum in step 1.2 and bounding every column sum by $C$ from step 1.1 gives $\lVert Ax\rVert_1\le\sum_{j<n}\bigl(\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|\bigr)|x_j|\le C\sum_{j<n}|x_j|=C\lVert x\rVert_1$. [step 1.2, step 1.1, L1, algebra]

2.2 Choose $j^{\ast}<n$ attaining the maximum column sum, so $\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij^{\ast}}|=C$, which exists by step 1.1. [step 1.1, choose]

2.3 For every $i<m$, $|(Ax)_i|=|\sum_{j<n}a_{ij}x_j|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le R\lVert x\rVert_\infty$, using the triangle inequality, $|x_j|\le\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ and the definition of $R$. [L1, step 1.3, algebra]

2.4 Choose $i^{\ast}<m$ attaining the maximum row sum: $\sum_{j<n}|a_{i^{\ast}j}|=R$, which exists by step 1.3. [step 1.3, choose]

3.1 By [L2] the induced norm is the supremum of the ratio over nonzero $x$, so step 2.1 gives $\lVert A\rVert_1\le C$. [step 2.1, L2]

3.2 For the standard basis vector $e_{j^{\ast}}$ of [L3], $\lVert e_{j^{\ast}}\rVert_1=1$ and $\lVert Ae_{j^{\ast}}\rVert_1=\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij^{\ast}}|=C$, so the ratio $\lVert Ae_{j^{\ast}}\rVert_1/\lVert e_{j^{\ast}}\rVert_1=C$ is attained and $\lVert A\rVert_1\ge C$. [L1, L3, step 2.2]

3.3 Taking the maximum over $i<m$ in step 2.3 gives $\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le R\lVert x\rVert_\infty$, and by [L2] the induced $\infty$-norm is at most $R$. [step 2.3, L1, L2]

3.4 Define $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ by $x_j:=1$ when $a_{i^{\ast}j}\ge 0$ and $x_j:=-1$ when $a_{i^{\ast}j}<0$; then $\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1$ and $(Ax)_{i^{\ast}}=\sum_{j<n}a_{i^{\ast}j}x_j=\sum_{j<n}|a_{i^{\ast}j}|=R$, by [L1] and [L3]. [L1, L3, step 2.4, algebra]

4.1 Steps 3.1 and 3.2 give $\lVert A\rVert_1=C$, which is claim 1. [step 3.1, step 3.2]

4.2 The vector $x$ of step 3.4 attains the ratio $R$, so $\lVert A\rVert_\infty\ge R$; with step 3.3 this gives $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=R$, which is claim 2. [step 3.4, step 3.3, L2]

5.1 Claims 1 and 2 are steps 4.1 and 4.2. [step 4.1, step 4.2] ∎

## Statement

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over
entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication.
Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes,

$$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$

$$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$

$$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

These identities include every zero-sized shape.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A field $F$; matrices $A\in M_{m\times n}(F)$, $B\in M_{n\times p}(F)$, and $C\in M_{p\times q}(F)$; conformable matrices $A',B'$; and a scalar $\lambda\in F$.

[L1] Matrix products and identity matrices are defined entrywise by finite row-by-column sums ([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]).

[L2] A finite double sum may be evaluated in either order ([[lem-finite-sum-reindexing-and-fubini]]).

## Proof

**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 For $i<m$ and $\ell<q$, expansion by [L1] gives $((AB)C)_{i\ell}=\sum_{k<p}\sum_{j<n}(a_{ij}b_{jk})c_{k\ell}$ and $(A(BC))_{i\ell}=\sum_{j<n}\sum_{k<p}a_{ij}(b_{jk}c_{k\ell})$. [given, L1]

2.1 Associativity and distributivity in $F$, followed by [L2], identify the two sums in step 1.1, so $(AB)C=A(BC)$. [step 1.1, L1, L2]

3.1 The entry formulas also give $(I_mA)_{ik}=a_{ik}=(AI_n)_{ik}$; splitting sums gives both distributive laws; pulling out $\lambda$ gives scalar compatibility; and a sum of zero summands gives each zero law. Thus all stated identities hold entrywise. [step 2.1, L1]

4.1 If any indexing dimension is zero, every asserted matrix equality either has no entries to compare or reduces to an empty sum, whose value is $0$. Hence the same calculations cover all zero-sized shapes, including $I_0$. [step 3.1, L1, L2] ∎

## Statement

Under the input conditions of [[alg-xd-finite-budget-adaptive-projection]], the algorithm terminates after at most $N$ projection attempts and at most $NB$ uniformization terms. If it returns `certified` for $F_i$, then the true killed loss $c_{F_i}(T)$ is at most $\varepsilon$, the embedded killed-vector $\ell^1$ error is at most $\varepsilon$, and every bounded observable with oscillation $\operatorname{osc}(f)$ has cemetery-lift error at most $\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)\varepsilon$. An `inconclusive` return makes no claim that any finite projection meets the tolerance.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite nested candidate list $F_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq F_N$, a finite term cap $B$, a tolerance $\varepsilon>0$, and valid projection-rate and arithmetic certificates as required by the algorithm.

[F1] [[alg-xd-finite-budget-adaptive-projection]]: each candidate is attempted at most once, solver terms are capped by $B$, and `certified` is returned only when a validated upper endpoint $U_i$ satisfies $U_i\le\varepsilon$.

[F2] [[thm-xd-finite-state-projection-loss-and-observable-bound]]: for each actual projection, its cemetery mass is the exit probability, the embedded killed-vector $\ell^1$ error equals that mass, and the bounded-observable error is at most half the oscillation times that mass.

[F3] [[thm-xd-uniformization-truncation-and-error]]: a computed finite cemetery vector with certified total error $\delta_i$ has each coordinate within $\delta_i$ of the exact coordinate.

## Proof


**Proof technique:** verify the finite loop bound and the interval certificate.

1.1 The procedure iterates over only the supplied finite list $F_1,\ldots,F_N$, and for each $F_i$ the uniformization solver uses at most $B$ terms by [F1]. It either returns during one of these calls or after the last candidate, so it terminates after at most $N$ projections and $NB$ terms. [given, F1, algebra]

1.2 Suppose the algorithm returns `certified` at index $i$. By [F3], $|\widehat c_i-c_{F_i}(T)|\le\delta_i$. Since $0\le c_{F_i}(T)\le1$, the interval endpoints in [F1] enclose $c_{F_i}(T)$; hence $c_{F_i}(T)\le U_i\le\varepsilon$. [F1, F3, algebra]

2.1 Apply [F2] to this actual $F_i$: the embedded killed-vector error equals $c_{F_i}(T)$ and the observable error is at most $\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_{F_i}(T)$. Step 1.2 gives the asserted $\varepsilon$ bounds. [F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 If no candidate passes, or a finite solver returns an unavailable certificate, [F1] specifies `inconclusive`; the procedure has examined only the supplied finite list and therefore establishes no existence claim for a projection outside that list. [F1, given] ∎

## Statement

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite column generator $Q$, a column probability vector $p_0$, time $t\ge0$, and an admissible uniformization rate $\nu\ge0$.

[F1] [[def-xd-finite-column-generator]]: $Q$ has nonnegative off-diagonal entries, zero column sums, and exit rates $r_j=-q_{jj}$.

[F2] [[lem-xd-uniformized-matrix-is-stochastic]]: if $\nu>0$ dominates every exit rate, $P=I+Q/\nu$ is column stochastic; if $\nu=0$, $Q=0$.

[F3] [[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]]: for $\lambda\ge0$, the Poisson mass at $k$ is $e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k/k!$ when $\lambda>0$ and the law is concentrated at zero when $\lambda=0$.

[F4] [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]: the finite-parameter Poisson masses sum to one.

[F5] [[lem-xd-finite-matrix-exponential-series]]: $e^{tQ}$ has its locally convergent factorial series, derivative $Qe^{tQ}$, and the commuting-matrix product identity.

[F6] [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: a real function continuous on a closed interval and differentiable on its interior has endpoint difference equal to its derivative at some interior point times the interval length.

[F7] [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]: finite sums and products of differentiable real-valued functions obey the sum and product rules, applied entrywise to finite matrix-vector products.

## Proof


**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Suppose $\nu>0$. By [F2], $P$ is nonnegative and column stochastic. If $x$ is a column probability vector, then $Px$ is nonnegative and $\sum_i(Px)_i=\sum_j(\sum_iP_{ij})x_j=\sum_jx_j=1$. Induction gives that $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector for every $k\ge0$. [given, F1, F2, algebra, induction]

1.2 By [F3] and the matrix series of [F5], the uniformization sum equals $e^{-\nu t}e^{\nu tP}p_0$. The power series gives $e^{-\nu tI}=e^{-\nu t}I$; since $-\nu tI$ commutes with $\nu tP$, [F5] gives $e^{-\nu tI}e^{\nu tP}=e^{\nu t(P-I)}=e^{tQ}$ using $Q=\nu(P-I)$. This proves the displayed identity. [F2, F3, F5, algebra]

1.3 By [F5], $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$ has derivative $Qe^{tQ}p_0=Qp(t)$ and initial value $p_0$. [given, F5, algebra]

1.4 Let $u$ be any other differentiable solution with the same initial vector and put $z(t)=e^{-tQ}u(t)$. The product rule [F7], the equation $u'=Qu$, and commutation of $Q$ with $e^{-tQ}$ from [F5] give $z'(t)=0$. If $t>0$, [F6] applied to each coordinate of $z$ on $[0,t]$ gives $z(t)=z(0)=p_0$; if $t=0$ this follows from the initial value directly. Multiplying by $e^{tQ}$ and using [F5] gives $u(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. Thus the solution is unique. [given, F5, F6, F7, algebra]

2.1 The weights in [F3] at parameter $\nu t$ sum to one by [F4]. Hence the nonnegative weighted sum of the probability vectors from step 1.1 is itself a probability vector. [given, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $\nu=0$, [F2] gives $Q=0$. The constant function $p(t)=p_0$ solves the equation. The uniqueness argument in step 1.4 applied with $Q=0$ shows that every solution with this initial value equals it. This proves the zero-rate case. [given, F2, step 1.4, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $X_t$ be a given nonexplosive countable chain with rates $q(x,y)$, initial law $p_0$, and finite exit rates as in [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]]. For a finite nonempty $F\subseteq S$, let $\tau_F$ and $Y_t$ be the killed projection of [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]. Write $p_t(x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x)$ and $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(Y_t=x)$ for $x\in F$. Then

$$u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x),\qquad c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t).$$

If $\bar u_F$ is $u_F$ extended by zero to $S\setminus F$, then

$$\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}=c_F(t).$$

For any bounded real observable $f:S\to\mathbb R$, put $\operatorname{osc}(f):=\sup_{x\in S}f(x)-\inf_{x\in S}f(x)$ and extend it to the cemetery state by $f(\dagger):=(\sup f+\inf f)/2$. The corresponding expectation error obeys

$$|\mathbb E[f(X_t)]-\mathbb E[f(Y_t)]|\le\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t).$$

The finite cemetery lift $\widetilde Q_F$ in [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]] is a finite generator and $\mathcal L(Y_t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\mathcal L(Y_0)$. A path that exits $F$ and later returns contributes to the full marginal but remains at the cemetery state in the killed projection.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** An already-given nonexplosive time-homogeneous pure-jump chain $X_t$ on a countable set $S$, its finite transition rates, an initial probability law $p_0$, and a finite nonempty subset $F\subseteq S$.

[F1] [[def-xd-countable-nonexplosive-ctmc]]: at state $x$, the holding time has rate $\lambda(x)=\sum_{y\ne x}q(x,y)$ and the next-state probability is $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$; the process is Markov and nonexplosive.

[F2] [[def-xd-finite-state-projection-and-cemetery-lift]]: $Y_t=X_t$ before the first exit from $F$ and $Y_t=\dagger$ from that exit onward; its finite rate matrix is $\widetilde Q_F$.

[F3] [[thm-xd-finite-generator-master-equation-uniformization]]: for a finite column generator and initial probability vector, the unique master-equation solution is its matrix exponential.

[F4] [[def-xd-countable-l1-distance]]: for a probability mass $p$ and subprobability mass $u$, $\|p-u\|_{\ell^1(S)}=\sum_{x\in S}|p(x)-u(x)|$ is finite.

[F5] [[lem-exponential-dominates-one-plus-x]]: $1+x\le e^x$ for every real $x$.

[F6] [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]: $e^x=\sum_{k\ge0}x^k/k!$ and this series converges absolutely for every real $x$.

## Proof


**Proof technique:** identify the finite killed chain, then compare it pathwise with the full chain.

1.1 For each source state $x\in F$, the off-diagonal entries of $\widetilde Q_F$ are the internal rates $q(x,y)$ and the exit rate to $\dagger$ is $\sum_{y\notin F}q(x,y)$. Their sum is $\lambda(x)$, so the diagonal $-\lambda(x)$ makes the column sum zero. The cemetery column is zero. Therefore $\widetilde Q_F$ is a finite column generator. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 By the definition of $Y$, for each $x\in F$ the event $\{Y_t=x\}$ is exactly $\{X_t=x,\tau_F>t\}$; the complementary event $\{Y_t=\dagger\}$ is $\{\tau_F\le t\}$. Therefore $u_F(t,x)=\mathbb P(X_t=x,\tau_F>t)\le p_t(x)$ and $c_F(t)=\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)$. Returning paths are included in $p_t$ but excluded from $u_F$ by the strict first-exit condition. [F1, F2, given]

2.1 Let $M_F=\max_{x\in F}\lambda(x)$, finite because $F$ is finite. For $0\le h\le1$, [F6] bounds the exponential series remainder by $|e^{-\lambda(x)h}-(1-\lambda(x)h)|\le h^2\sum_{k\ge2}\lambda(x)^k/k!$, so no-jump probability is $1-\lambda(x)h+o(h)$ uniformly on finite $F$. If $\lambda(x)>0$, the first-jump probability $1-e^{-\lambda(x)h}=\lambda(x)h+o(h)$ multiplied by the destination probability $q(x,y)/\lambda(x)$ from [F1] gives rate $q(x,y)h+o(h)$ for each $y\ne x$; if $\lambda(x)=0$, all rates from $x$ are zero and these probabilities are zero. For the aggregate exit event, its conditional destination probability is $a_x/\lambda(x)$ when $\lambda(x)>0$, so its probability is $a_xh+o(h)$; when $\lambda(x)=0$, $a_x=0$ and this probability is zero. Here $a_x=\lambda(x)-\sum_{y\in F,y\ne x}q(x,y)\ge0$. After reaching $\dagger$ there are no further changes. By [F5] applied to $-u$, $1-e^{-u}\le u$ for $u\ge0$, so the probability of a first change within $h$ is at most $M_Fh$; conditional on a first change that stays in $F$, a second change within the remaining time has probability at most $M_Fh$. Hence the probability of two or more changes is at most $M_F^2h^2$. Thus the finite transition matrix of $Y$ is $I+h\widetilde Q_F+o(h)$ as $h\downarrow0$, uniformly over its finite state space. [F1, F2, F5, F6, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Extend $u_F$ by zero outside $F$. For $x\in F$, $p_t(x)-u_F(t,x)\ge0$ by step 1.2; for $x\notin F$, the difference is $p_t(x)\ge0$. Summing these nonnegative differences over $S$ gives $1-\sum_{x\in F}u_F(t,x)=1-\mathbb P(\tau_F>t)=c_F(t)$. By [F4], this sum is exactly $\|p_t-\bar u_F(t)\|_{\ell^1(S)}$. [F2, F4, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The process $Y$ is Markov: before killing this follows from the Markov property of $X$, and after killing its state $\dagger$ is absorbing. Hence its finite column transition matrix $T_Y(h)$ satisfies $T_Y(h)=I+h\widetilde Q_F+o(h)$ entrywise by step 2.1, and its law satisfies $\widetilde p(t+h)=T_Y(h)\widetilde p(t)$. This gives the right derivative $\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p(t)$. For $t>0$, $\widetilde p(t)=T_Y(h)\widetilde p(t-h)$. Since the state space has finitely many coordinates, the entrywise expansion and $\sum_j\widetilde p_j(t-h)=1$ imply each coordinate of $\widetilde p(t)-\widetilde p(t-h)$ is $O(h)$; hence $\widetilde p(t-h)\to\widetilde p(t)$. Dividing the identity by $h$ and using the entrywise limit $(T_Y(h)-I)/h\to\widetilde Q_F$ gives the left derivative $\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p(t)$ as well, because every coordinate is a finite sum. Thus $\widetilde p'=\widetilde Q_F\widetilde p$ with initial law $\widetilde p(0)$. By [F3], $\widetilde p(t)=e^{t\widetilde Q_F}\widetilde p(0)$. [F1, F2, F3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Let $a=\inf f$, $b=\sup f$, and $c=(a+b)/2=f(\dagger)$. The coupling uses the same path $X$: on $\{\tau_F>t\}$, $Y_t=X_t$, and on $\{\tau_F\le t\}$, $Y_t=\dagger$. Thus $|\mathbb E f(X_t)-\mathbb E f(Y_t)|=|\mathbb E[\mathbf1_{\{\tau_F\le t\}}(f(X_t)-c)]|\le\tfrac12(b-a)\mathbb P(\tau_F\le t)=\tfrac12\operatorname{osc}(f)c_F(t)$, as asserted. [F2, step 1.2, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator, $p_0$ a column probability vector, and $\nu>0$ an admissible rate. For $\lambda=\nu t$ and $K\ge0$, the exact one-series partial sum

$$u_K(t):=\sum_{k=0}^{K}e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!}P^kp_0$$

is nonnegative and substochastic, and its exact $\ell^1$ distance from $p(t)$ is the scalar Poisson tail $\tau_K(\lambda)=\mathbb P(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)>K)$. If $\nu t>0$, the budgeted algorithm sets $m=\lceil\nu t\rceil$ and $\mu=\nu t/m\le1$, and uses $R_{\mu,K}=\sum_{k=0}^K e^{-\mu}\mu^kP^k/k!$. Then $R_{\mu,K}^m p_0$ is nonnegative and substochastic, and its exact transient $\ell^1$ error is

$$1-\left(\sum_{k=0}^{K}e^{-\mu}\frac{\mu^k}{k!}\right)^m\le m\tau_K(\mu)\le mG_K(\mu).$$

If a computed vector $\widehat u$ has a separately certified accumulated arithmetic/algebraic error $E_{\rm alg}:=\|\widehat u-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1$, then $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le mG_K(\mu)+E_{\rm alg}$. In rounded arithmetic, if $T$ is a validated upper bound for $mG_K(\mu)$, then $\|p(t)-\widehat u\|_1\le T+E_{\rm alg}$. The geometric tail certificate is not obtained by floating-point subtraction from one.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A finite column generator $Q$, a probability vector $p_0$, an admissible $\nu>0$, $t\ge0$, and a finite truncation index $K$.

[F1] [[lem-xd-uniformized-matrix-is-stochastic]]: $P=I+Q/\nu$ is nonnegative and column stochastic.

[F2] [[thm-xd-finite-generator-master-equation-uniformization]]: $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$ and $e^{tQ}=\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\nu t}(\nu t)^kP^k/k!$.

[F3] [[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] and [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]: the weights $w_k(\mu)=e^{-\mu}\mu^k/k!$ are nonnegative and sum to one.

[F4] [[lem-xd-geometric-poisson-tail-bound]]: $\tau_K(\mu)\le G_K(\mu)$ when $\mu<K+2$.

[F5] [[def-p-norms-on-rn]]: the vector $1$-norm is $\|x\|_1=\sum_i|x_i|$.

[F6] [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]], [[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]], and [[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]]: for a nonnegative matrix, its induced $1$-norm is its maximum column sum and induced matrix norms are submultiplicative.

[F7] [[alg-xd-budgeted-uniformization-accumulation]]: with $m$ substeps, the exact truncated vector is $R_{\mu,K}^mp_0$, the term count is at most $B$, rounded output carries a validated tail upper bound $T\ge mG_K(\mu)$, and any approximate vector carries its separate $E_{\rm alg}$ bound.

[F8] [[lem-xd-finite-matrix-exponential-series]]: $e^{sQ}e^{tQ}=e^{(s+t)Q}$ for real $s,t$.

## Proof


**Proof technique:** compare the full stochastic operator with its substochastic partial sum.

1.1 For any $\mu>0$, set $S_\mu=e^{\mu Q/\nu}=e^{-\mu}e^{\mu P}$ and $R_{\mu,K}=\sum_{k=0}^K w_k(\mu)P^k$. By [F1], each $P^k$ is nonnegative and column stochastic; [F2] and [F3] give $S_\mu=\sum_{k\ge0}w_k(\mu)P^k$ with nonnegative weights summing to one. Thus $R_{\mu,K}$ is nonnegative with common column sum $s_K:=\sum_{k=0}^K w_k(\mu)\le1$, and $S_\mu-R_{\mu,K}$ is nonnegative with common column sum $\tau_K(\mu)$. [F1, F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 The induced norm formula [F6] gives $\|S_\mu\|_1=1$, $\|R_{\mu,K}\|_1=s_K$, and $\|S_\mu-R_{\mu,K}\|_1=\tau_K(\mu)$. If $\lambda=\nu t=0$, only the $k=0$ Poisson weight is nonzero, so $p(t)=u_K(t)=p_0$ and the omitted mass is zero. If $\lambda>0$, apply step 1.1 with $\mu=\lambda$: $(S_\lambda-R_{\lambda,K})p_0$ is nonnegative and its coordinate sum is $\tau_K(\lambda)$; by [F5], the exact one-series $\ell^1$ omitted mass is therefore exactly the scalar Poisson tail. [F1, F2, F3, F5, F6, step 1.1]

3.1 In the time-split algorithm, $0<\mu\le1$ and $K\ge0$, so $\mu<K+2$ and [F4] gives $\tau_K(\mu)\le G_K(\mu)$. For $m$ substeps the telescoping identity $S_\mu^m-R_{\mu,K}^m=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}S_\mu^{m-1-j}(S_\mu-R_{\mu,K})R_{\mu,K}^j$, [F5]–[F6], and step 2.1 give $\|S_\mu^m-R_{\mu,K}^m\|_1\le m\tau_K(\mu)\le mG_K(\mu)$. [F4, F5, F6, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 Every term in the telescoping identity is nonnegative, so the exact vector error on $p_0$ is nonnegative. Each column sum of $S_\mu^m$ is one and each column sum of $R_{\mu,K}^m$ is $s_K^m$; hence its $\ell^1$ mass is exactly $1-s_K^m=1-(1-\tau_K(\mu))^m\le m\tau_K(\mu)$. This proves the exact time-split lost-mass identity and the preceding error bound. [F1, F3, F5, F6, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Since $m\mu=\nu t$, [F8] gives $S_\mu^m=e^{tQ}$ and [F2] gives $S_\mu^mp_0=p(t)$, while [F7] identifies the exact truncated output as $R_{\mu,K}^mp_0$. Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

When $n\ge1$, the following three displayed quantities are the same number:

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

**The value is a finite nonnegative real.** For $n\ge 1$ the norms
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

**The induced infinity norm is a separate named case.** When $m,n\ge1$, define

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

As in the rational-$p$ case, positive homogeneity gives

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

The supremum is finite because for every $i<m$ one has
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

**At $n=0$ the convention is explicit.** The only element of $\mathbb{R}^{0}$
is the zero vector, the only matrix $A\in M_{m\times 0}(\mathbb{R})$ is the
empty matrix, and the unit-ball definition gives $\lVert A\rVert_{p}=0$.
The unit sphere and the set of nonzero vectors are empty, so the two ratio
formulas above are not asserted in this case.

The induced quantity is a norm on the matrix space $M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$:
for each rational $p\ge1$, and likewise for the separately named
$\infty$-case when $m,n\ge1$, separation, absolute homogeneity and the triangle
inequality follow from the same three axioms of the underlying vector norm
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
For every real $x$, the series $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/\iota(n!)$ converges absolutely. Its power-series radius is therefore $+\infty$.

Matrix multiplication over a field is associative and unital, distributes over
entrywise addition on both sides, and is compatible with scalar multiplication.
Precisely, whenever the displayed products have compatible shapes,

$$A(BC)=(AB)C,\qquad I_mA=A=AI_n,$$

$$(A+A')B=AB+A'B,\qquad A(B+B')=AB+AB',$$

$$0B=0=A0,\qquad (\lambda A)B=\lambda(AB)=A(\lambda B).$$

These identities include every zero-sized shape.

**Natural exponents, in a monoid.** Let $(M,\cdot,e)$ be a monoid
([[def-semigroup-and-monoid]]) and $g \in M$. By the recursion theorem
([[thm-recursion]]), applied with the set $M$, the element $e$ and the function
$x \mapsto x \cdot g$ from $M$ to $M$, there is exactly one function
$\mathbb{N} \to M$, written $n \mapsto g^{n}$, with

$$g^{0} = e, \qquad g^{\sigma(n)} = g^{n} \cdot g \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

In particular $g^{0} = e$ for **every** $g$, including $g = e$, and
$g^{1} = g^{\sigma(0)} = e \cdot g = g$. Since $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$
([[def-natural-numbers]]), the exponent $0$ is a genuine value of the definition
and not a separate convention.

**Integer exponents, in a group.** Let $G$ be a group ([[def-group]]) and
$g \in G$. Write $\iota : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{Z}$ for the embedding
$\iota(k) = [(k,0)]$ of [[lem-nat-embeds-int]], which is injective, preserves
addition, multiplication and order, and has as image exactly the nonnegative
integers. For $x \in \mathbb{Z}$ define

- $g^{x} := g^{k}$, the natural power, when $0 \le x$ and $x = \iota(k)$;
- $g^{x} := (g^{k})^{-1}$ when $x < 0$ and $-x = \iota(k)$.

**Why this is well defined.** The order on $\mathbb{Z}$ is total and
antisymmetric ([[thm-int-ordered-ring]], [[def-int-order]]), so exactly one of
$0 \le x$ and $x < 0$ holds and the two clauses never both apply. In the first
clause $x$ is nonnegative, so $x = \iota(k)$ for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$, and $k$
is unique because $\iota$ is injective. In the second clause $x < 0$ gives
$0 = x + (-x) < 0 + (-x) = -x$ by compatibility of the order with addition
([[thm-int-ordered-ring]], [[def-int-operations]]), so $-x$ is a positive integer
and again $-x = \iota(k)$ for a unique $k$. The inverse $(g^{k})^{-1}$ is a single
determined element by [[lem-inverse-unique]] and [[def-invertible-element]].
Finally the two readings of $g^{\iota(k)}$, as a natural power and as an integer
power, agree by construction, so no ambiguity is introduced.

**Abbreviation.** In an exponent we write $k$ for the integer $\iota(k)$ when a
natural number $k$ is used where an integer is expected; this is unambiguous
because $\iota$ is injective and preserves the arithmetic and the order, and
because the two readings of $g^{k}$ agree as just noted.

**Additive notation.** When the group is written additively the same object is
written $n g$ or $n \cdot g$ rather than $g^{n}$, with $0 g = 0$ and
$\sigma(n) g = n g + g$; the definitions are identical, only the symbols differ.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\ge 1$ and $n\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, with the induced $1$-norm and the
separately defined induced $\infty$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Maximum column sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_1=\max_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|$.
2. **Maximum row sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$.

set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have

$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

before.claim: Put $M=\|A\|_1$. For any $T>0$ and $|t|\le T$, [F1] gives $\|t^kA^k/k!\|_1\le (TM)^k/k!$. The majorant series converges by [F2], so the matrix series is absolutely and uniformly Cauchy on $[-T,T]$ and defines $e^{tA}$. Since $T$ was arbitrary, it converges locally uniformly.

Fix $c\in\mathbb R$ and choose $R>|c|$. For $|h|<R-|c|$ and $k\ge1$, the finite factorization $(c+h)^k-c^k=h\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(c+h)^{k-1-j}c^j$ bounds both the norm of the $k$th matrix-series difference quotient and the norm of the $k$th proposed derivative term by $M(MR)^{k-1}/(k-1)!$. The sum of these bounds converges by [F2], so both tails are uniformly small; each finite partial sum is a matrix polynomial whose difference quotient tends to its ordinary derivative. Taking first a sufficiently large partial sum and then $h\to0$ proves differentiability and gives $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}|_{t=c}=\sum_{k\ge1}A^kc^{k-1}/(k-1)!=Ae^{cA}$.
Every term in the derivative series commutes with $A$, so the same sum equals $e^{cA}A$. The $k=0$ term in the defining series gives $e^{0A}=I$.

For commuting $A,B$, the double series for $e^Ae^B$ is absolutely convergent because its term norms are bounded by $\|A\|_1^m\|B\|_1^n/(m!n!)$, whose double sum is finite by [F2]. Regroup by $r=m+n$; commutation and the binomial formula give $\sum_{m+n=r}A^mB^n/(m!n!)=(A+B)^r/r!$. Summing over $r$ proves $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

after.claim: If $A$ has size $0\times0$, the matrix space has one element, which is both $0$ and $I_0$; every partial sum in the definition is this same matrix. Thus $e^{tA}=I_0$ for every $t$, its derivative is the zero matrix, and the derivative identities, initial value, and commuting-product identity all hold because every product and sum is the unique empty matrix. Hence assume below that $A$ has size $n\times n$ with $n\ge1$.

Put $M=\|A\|_1$. By induction using [F1] and [F4], $\|A^k\|_1\le M^k$ for every $k\ge0$. For $|t|\le T$, [F5] then bounds each entry of $t^kA^k/k!$ by $(TM)^k/k!$. The scalar majorant converges by [F2], so each entry series converges absolutely and uniformly on $[-T,T]$; its entrywise sums define a matrix $E(t)$. Each column has only $n$ entries, so the maximum-column-sum formula [F5] bounds the norm of a matrix tail by $n$ times the scalar majorant tail. Therefore the matrix series converges in induced $1$-norm uniformly on $[-T,T]$. Since $T$ was arbitrary, it converges locally uniformly and defines $e^{tA}=E(t)$.

Fix $c\in\mathbb R$ and choose $R>|c|$. If $|h|<R-|c|$, then $|c|,|c+h|<R$; for $k\ge1$, the factorization $(c+h)^k-c^k=h\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}(c+h)^{k-1-j}c^j$ bounds the norm of the $k$th matrix-series difference quotient by $M^kR^{k-1}/(k-1)!$, and the same bound holds for the $k$th proposed derivative term $c^{k-1}A^k/(k-1)!$. The sum of these bounds is $M\sum_{j\ge0}(MR)^j/j!<\infty$ by [F2]. For each finite partial sum, the factorization also shows that its difference quotient tends to the finite sum of the proposed derivative terms, using $(k+1)!=(k+1)k!$ from [F6]. For each fixed nonzero $h$, the full difference quotient is the limit of those of the finite partial sums by [step 1.2]; the two uniform tail bounds let us first choose a large partial sum and then take $h\to0$. Consequently $E$ is differentiable at $c$ and $E'(c)=\sum_{k\ge1}c^{k-1}A^k/(k-1)!$.

From [F3] and the recursive power definition [F4], induction gives $A^k=AA^{k-1}=A^{k-1}A$ for every $k\ge1$. Hence the derivative series in step 1.3 is the limit of both $A\sum_{j=0}^{N}c^jA^j/j!$ and $\bigl(\sum_{j=0}^{N}c^jA^j/j!\bigr)A$ as $N\to\infty$. Submultiplicativity [F1] makes multiplication by fixed $A$ continuous, so these limits are $AE(c)$ and $E(c)A$. At $c=0$, all positive-degree terms vanish and the constant term is $A^0=I_n$. Thus $E'(c)=AE(c)=E(c)A$ and $E(0)=I_n$.

Suppose $A,B\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ commute. For each $r\ge0$ set $D_r:=\sum_{m=0}^r A^mB^{r-m}/(m!(r-m)!)$. Induction from $AB=BA$ and [F3] gives $B^sA=AB^s$ for every $s\ge0$. Distributing $D_r(A+B)$ and using this commutation, the coefficient of $A^jB^{r+1-j}$ is $1/(j!(r-j)!)+1/((j-1)!(r+1-j)!)$ for $1\le j\le r$, which equals $(r+1)/(j!(r+1-j)!)$ by [F6]; for $j=0$ and $j=r+1$ the single endpoint coefficient has that same value by $(r+1)!=(r+1)r!$. Thus $D_r(A+B)=(r+1)D_{r+1}$. Since $D_0=I_n$, induction, the recursive power law [F4], and the nonzero factorial images in [F6] give $D_r=(A+B)^r/r!$ for every $r$.

Apply the power bound and convergence argument of step 1.2 to $B$ and $A+B$ as well. Put $a_m=\|A\|_1^m/m!$ and $b_n=\|B\|_1^n/n!$; both scalar series converge by [F2]. The finite product $E_N(A)E_N(B)$ expands by [F3] as the square sum over $0\le m,n\le N$ of $A^mB^n/(m!n!)$, whose term norms are at most $a_mb_n$ by [F1] and [F4]. Its difference from the triangular sum over $m+n\le N$ has norm at most $(\sum_{m>N/2}a_m)(\sum_n b_n)+(\sum_m a_m)(\sum_{n>N/2}b_n)$, which tends to zero; every omitted pair has $m>N/2$ or $n>N/2$. By step 1.2, $E_N(A)E_N(B)\to e^Ae^B$ (matrix multiplication is continuous by [F1]); by step 3.1 the triangular sum is $\sum_{r=0}^N(A+B)^r/r!$, which converges to $e^{A+B}$. Therefore $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

Step 1.1 covers the zero-sized matrix case. For $n\ge1$, steps 1.2 and 1.3 establish convergence and differentiation, step 2.1 gives the derivative identities and initial value, and steps 3.1–3.2 prove the commuting-product identity. Thus every claim in the Statement holds.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$

normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

**The factorial.** By the recursion theorem ([[thm-recursion]]) applied to the
set $\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$, the starting element $(0,1)$ and the function
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot \sigma(k))$, and by the same induction on the
first coordinate as in [[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]], there is a unique
$F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with

$$F(0) = 1, \qquad F(\sigma(n)) = F(n)\cdot\sigma(n) \quad (n \in \mathbb{N}).$$

We write $n! := F(n)$. Thus $0! = 1$, $1! = 0!\cdot 1 = 1$, $2! = 1!\cdot 2 = 2$,
$3! = 6$, $4! = 24$, $5! = 120$, $6! = 720$.

**$0! = 1$ is the base clause of this recursion**, not a convention imported from
elsewhere. Nothing about empty products is presupposed; the agreement with the
empty product is proved below, in clause (a), rather than assumed.

**Truncated difference.** Throughout, $n - k$ is the operation fixed in
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]: the unique $j$ with $k + j = n$ when
$k \le n$, and $0$ when $n < k$.

**The falling factorial.** For $n \in \mathbb{N}$ define $n^{\underline{k}}$ by
recursion on $k$, by the recursion theorem applied to
$\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}$ with starting element $(0,1)$ and
$f(k, v) = (\sigma(k),\, v \cdot (n-k))$:

$$n^{\underline{0}} = 1, \qquad n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k) .$$

So $n^{\underline{1}} = 1\cdot(n-0) = n$ and $n^{\underline{2}} = n\,(n-1)$, and
for $k \le n$ the value is the product $n(n-1)\cdots(n-k+1)$ of the $k$ topmost
factors.

**Four facts, proved here because the page uses each of them.**

**(a) The factorial is the product of the first $n$ positive naturals.**
$n! = \prod_{j<n}\sigma(j) = \prod_{j<n}(j+1)$, the $\mathbb{N}$-valued product of
[[def-nat-finite-sum-and-product]]. Induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]): at
$n = 0$ both sides are $1$, the empty product and the base clause agreeing; and
$\prod_{j<\sigma(n)}\sigma(j) = \big(\prod_{j<n}\sigma(j)\big)\cdot\sigma(n) = n!\cdot\sigma(n) = \sigma(n)!$.
**So the empty-product reading and the base-clause reading are the same reading**,
and neither was assumed.

**(b) $n! \ne 0$, and $\iota(n!) = \prod^{\mathbb{R}}_{j<n}\iota(j+1)$.** For the
first, $0! = 1 \ne 0$ ([[thm-omega-is-peano-system]]) and
$\sigma(n)! = n!\cdot\sigma(n)$ is a product of two nonzero naturals, which is
nonzero: if $xy = 0$ with $y \ne 0$ then $xy = 0\cdot y$
([[lem-nat-mult-identity]]) and cancellation gives $x = 0$
([[lem-nat-mult-cancellative]]). So $n! \ne 0$ for every $n$ by induction. For the second, apply the bridge clause
6 of that lemma to clause (a) above. This is what makes the factorial of this
page and the real-valued product $\prod_{j<n}(j+1)$ used elsewhere in the library
**one object seen twice**, rather than two unrelated notions.

**(c) $n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$ for $k \le n$.** Induction on $k$, for
all $n$ at once. At $k = 0$ this reads $1 \cdot n! = n!$. Assume it at $k$ and
let $\sigma(k) \le n$; then $k \le n$, and writing $d := n - k$ we have
$k + d = n$ and $d \ne 0$, since $k + 0 = k \ne n$; so $d = \sigma(e)$ for a
unique $e$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]), and $\sigma(k) + e = n$, that is
$e = n - \sigma(k)$ ([[lem-nat-add-cancellative]]). Therefore
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}}\cdot\big(n-\sigma(k)\big)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)\cdot e! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\big(e!\cdot\sigma(e)\big) = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot\sigma(e)! = n^{\underline{k}}\cdot(n-k)! = n!$,
using commutativity and associativity of multiplication
([[lem-nat-mult-associative]], [[lem-nat-mult-commutative]]) and the recursion
clause for the factorial.

**(d) Boundary values.** $n^{\underline{0}} = 1$ for every $n$, by the base
clause; $n^{\underline{n}} = n!$, since clause (c) at $k = n$ gives
$n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0! = n!$ and $0! = 1$; and
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ whenever $k > n$. For the last, $n - n = 0$ gives
$n^{\underline{\sigma(n)}} = n^{\underline{n}}\cdot 0 = 0$, the clause
$x \cdot 0 = 0$ being definitional ([[def-nat-multiplication]]), and if
$n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ then
$n^{\underline{\sigma(k)}} = 0$ as well, so $n^{\underline{k}} = 0$ for every
$k \ge \sigma(n)$ by induction.

1. If $|r| < 1$ then the series $\sum r^k$ converges ([[def-series]]) and

Let $S=\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}$ with $n\ge1$. Identify its real matrices with $M_n(\mathbb R)$, the finite matrix space with row and column indices in $S$ from [[def-matrix-space]], and use the matrix-product and identity conventions of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]. A **finite column generator** on $S$ is a real matrix $Q=(q_{ij})\in M_n(\mathbb R)$ satisfying

$$q_{ij}\ge0\quad(i\ne j),\qquad \sum_{i<n}q_{ij}=0\quad(j<n).$$

The column index $j$ is the source state and the row index $i$ is the destination state: for $i\ne j$, $q_{ij}$ is the transition rate from $j$ to $i$. The exit rate from $j$ is

$$r_j:=-q_{jj}=\sum_{i\ne j}q_{ij}\ge0.$$

A **column probability vector** is $p\in\mathbb R^n$ with $p_i\ge0$ for each $i$ and $\sum_{i<n}p_i=1$. A **subprobability vector** has the same coordinatewise nonnegativity and has coordinate sum at most one. These conventions are used throughout this page.

Let $Q$ be a finite column generator and let $\nu\ge\max_{j<n}r_j$. If $\nu>0$, then

$$P:=I+Q/\nu$$

has nonnegative entries and every column sums to one. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$.

$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

For a finite real square matrix $A$, define

$$e^{tA}:=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^kA^k}{k!}.$$

This series converges absolutely and uniformly for $t$ in every bounded interval. It is differentiable with $\frac{d}{dt}e^{tA}=Ae^{tA}=e^{tA}A$ and $e^{0A}=I$. If finite square matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, then $e^Ae^B=e^{A+B}$.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

For $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$ with $\mu\ge0$ and integer $K\ge0$, write $\tau_K(\mu):=\mathbb P(N>K)$. If $\mu=0$, then $\tau_K(\mu)=0$. If $\mu>0$ and $\mu<K+2$, then

$$\tau_K(\mu)\le \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}.$$

The right side is a geometric majorant computed from a Poisson mass, not a floating-point subtraction of a rounded partial sum from one.

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real matrix
([[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]]), regarded as the linear map
$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$ with $m\ge 1$ and $n\ge 1$, and let
$A=(a_{ij})\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$, with the induced $1$-norm and the
separately defined induced $\infty$-norm of
[[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Maximum column sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_1=\max_{j<n}\sum_{i<m}|a_{ij}|$.
2. **Maximum row sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$
3. **Normalisation.** For every $n\ge 1$,
   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$
   where $I_n$ is the identity matrix of [[def-matrix-product-and-identity-matrix]];
   at $n=0$ the unique empty matrix $I_0\in M_0(\mathbb{R})$ has
   $\lVert I_0\rVert_p=0$, the convention of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

**Inputs.** A finite column generator $Q$, a column probability vector $p_0$, $t\ge0$, an admissible rate $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, a positive tail budget $\varepsilon$, a positive integer total-term cap $B$, and either exact real arithmetic or a validated arithmetic backend. In a rounded execution, the backend must certify the scalar control decisions defining $m$ and $\mu$, each finite tail-budget comparison, and an outward upper bound $T\ge mG_K(\mu)$; it must also return a certified $\ell^1$ error bound $E_{\rm alg}:=\|\widehat p-R_{\mu,K}^mp_0\|_1$ for its computed vector. The vector bound includes any arithmetic error from the weights, time split, and matrix-free $P$ actions. If any scalar or vector certificate is unavailable, return `certificate-unavailable`.

**Outputs.** Return $(p_0,0,0)$ when $\nu=0$ or $t=0$. Otherwise return `budget-exhausted` or `certificate-unavailable`, or an approximate vector $\widehat p$ and certified bounds $(T,E_{\rm alg})$ for which $\|p(t)-\widehat p\|_1\le T+E_{\rm alg}$. Here $T\ge mG_K(\mu)$ is an outward-certified Poisson-tail upper bound and $E_{\rm alg}$ bounds the arithmetic/algebraic error relative to the exact truncated accumulation. In exact real arithmetic, $T=mG_K(\mu)$ and $E_{\rm alg}=0$.

**Procedure.** For $\nu t>0$, set $m=\lceil\nu t\rceil$ and $\mu=\nu t/m$, so $0<\mu\le1$. A rounded backend must certify these values and inequalities; if it cannot, return `certificate-unavailable`. If $m>B$, return `budget-exhausted`. Set $K_{\max}=\lfloor B/m\rfloor-1$. Search the finite list $K=0,1,\ldots,K_{\max}$ for a member satisfying

$$G_K(\mu):=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}\le\varepsilon/m.$$

In rounded arithmetic, accept a candidate only when a validated upper enclosure proves the displayed inequality, and set $T$ to a validated upper bound for $mG_K(\mu)$. If no candidate works, return `budget-exhausted` when the comparisons certify that every candidate fails, and `certificate-unavailable` when they do not decide the search. In exact arithmetic set $T=mG_K(\mu)$. Set $P=I+Q/\nu$ and $x_0=p_0$. For each substep $j=1,\ldots,m$, initialize $v_0=x_{j-1}$, $w_0=e^{-\mu}$, and $x_j=w_0v_0$. For $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, update

$$v_{k+1}=Pv_k,\qquad w_{k+1}=w_k\frac{\mu}{k+1},\qquad x_j\leftarrow x_j+w_{k+1}v_{k+1}.$$

These $P$ actions use the exact operator-application interface of [[def-matrix-free-access-model-for-krylov-methods]]: the routine supplies $v\mapsto Pv$ and vector additions and scalar multiples, without requiring stored matrix entries. Let $Q$ be a finite column generator and let $\nu\ge\max_{j<n}r_j$. If $\nu>0$, then

$$P:=I+Q/\nu$$

has nonnegative entries and every column sums to one. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$.

Let $Q$ be an $n\times n$ finite column generator, let $p_0$ be a column probability vector, and let $t\ge0$. The unique differentiable solution of

$$p'(t)=Qp(t),\qquad p(0)=p_0,$$

is $p(t)=e^{tQ}p_0$. If $\nu>0$ and $\nu\ge\max_jr_j$, put $P=I+Q/\nu$; then

$$p(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}e^{-\nu t}\frac{(\nu t)^k}{k!}P^kp_0.$$

Each term $P^kp_0$ is a probability vector, and the displayed Poisson mixture is a probability vector. If $\nu=0$, then $Q=0$ and $p(t)=p_0$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a Poisson point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

For $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)$ with $\mu\ge0$ and integer $K\ge0$, write $\tau_K(\mu):=\mathbb P(N>K)$. If $\mu=0$, then $\tau_K(\mu)=0$. If $\mu>0$ and $\mu<K+2$, then

$$\tau_K(\mu)\le \frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}.$$

The right side is a geometric majorant computed from a Poisson mass, not a floating-point subtraction of a rounded partial sum from one.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ be the function space of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]], with $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$.

### The $p$-norm, for a rational exponent $p \ge 1$

Let $p \in \mathbb{Q}$ with $p \ge 1$. For $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_p \;:=\; \Bigl(\sum_{k<n} |x_k|^{p}\Bigr)^{1/p},$$

where $|\cdot|$ is the absolute value ([[def-abs-value]]), the sum is the finite
sum of [[def-finite-sum]], and both powers are the **rational** powers of
[[def-rational-power]].

**Every power written here is defined.** Each base $|x_k|$ is a nonnegative real
and $p > 0$, so $|x_k|^{p}$ is given by [[def-rational-power]] for $|x_k| > 0$
and by its supplementary clause $0^{p} = 0$ for $|x_k| = 0$; the sum of these
nonnegative terms is nonnegative ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), and
$1/p$ is a positive rational, so the outer power is defined for the same two
reasons. The value does not depend on which representative of $p$ or of $1/p$ is
used ([[lem-rational-power-well-defined]]).

**The exponent is rational in this definition.**
[[def-rational-power]] supplies the nonnegative-base powers used here, and
[[thm-minkowski-finite]] supplies the corresponding triangle inequality for
rational $p \ge 1$. This item makes no claim with $p$ ranging over a real
interval; its rational domain is unchanged.

### The maximum norm

For $n \ge 1$ and $x \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ put

$$\lVert x\rVert_\infty \;:=\; \max\{\, |x_k| \;:\; k < n \,\},$$

the maximum of a nonempty finite set of reals, which exists and is one of its
elements ([[lem-finite-set-has-max]], [[def-max-min]]).

**The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is required and propagates.** At $n = 0$ the set
$\{|x_k| : k<n\}$ is empty and has no maximum ([[def-max-min]]). This is the same
restriction the published [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] carries, for the same reason, and
**every statement on this page that mentions $\lVert\cdot\rVert_\infty$ inherits
it**. The $p$-norms for rational $p \ge 1$ carry no such restriction: at $n = 0$
each is the empty sum raised to a positive rational power, hence $0$.

### The three cases the rest of the page uses

- $\lVert x\rVert_1 = \sum_{k<n}|x_k|$, since $t^{1} = t$ for $t \ge 0$
  ([[lem-rational-power-laws]], and $0^{1} = 0$ by the supplementary clause).
- $\lVert x\rVert_2 = \bigl(\sum_{k<n}|x_k|^{2}\bigr)^{1/2} = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}x_k^{2}}$,
  which is exactly the Euclidean norm of [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: the
  exponent $2$ agrees with the integer power, so $|x_k|^{2} = x_k^{2}$
  ([[lem-of-abs-value]]), and $t^{1/2}$ is the unique nonnegative square root of
  $t$, which is $\sqrt{t}$ ([[def-rational-power]], [[thm-of-square-roots]]).
  **The two notations denote the same function and no second Euclidean norm is
  introduced.**
- $\lVert x\rVert_\infty$ as above, for $n \ge 1$.

that the metrics they induce are exactly the published $d_1$, $d_2$ and
$d_\infty$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], is
[[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]; it is proved there
and is not assumed here.

Let $m,n\in\mathbb{N}$, let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$, and let

$x\mapsto Ax$ from $\mathbb{R}^{n}$ to $\mathbb{R}^{m}$ with the published
$p$-norms ([[def-p-norms-on-rn]]). The **matrix $p$-norm induced by**
$\lVert\cdot\rVert_{p}$ is

$$\lVert A\rVert_{p}\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_{p}\;:\;x\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\ \lVert x\rVert_{p}\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

$$\lVert A\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_p=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_p=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_p}{\lVert x\rVert_p},$$

the equalities following from positive homogeneity of $\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$
([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]], axiom (N2)) and
the equality $\lVert 0\rVert_p=0$.

$\lVert\cdot\rVert_p$ and $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ are equivalent by
[[thm-all-norms-on-rn-are-equivalent]], so there is $C>0$ with
$\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\lVert x\rVert_p$ for every $x$. For every $i<m$,
$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le C\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_p$,
so $\lVert Ax\rVert_p\le \bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C\lVert x\rVert_p$;
hence the supremum over the unit ball is at most the finite constant
$\bigl(\sum_{i<m}(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|)^{p}\bigr)^{1/p}C$.

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty\;:=\;\sup\Bigl\{\,\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\;:\;x\in\mathbb R^n,\ \lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1\,\Bigr\}.$$

$$\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty\le 1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{\lVert x\rVert_\infty=1}\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty=\sup_{x\ne 0}\frac{\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty}{\lVert x\rVert_\infty}.$$

$|(Ax)_i|\le\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,|x_j|\le\bigl(\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\bigr)\lVert x\rVert_\infty$,
so

$$\lVert Ax\rVert_\infty\le\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|\,\lVert x\rVert_\infty.$$

formulas above are not asserted in this case.

([[lem-p-norms-are-norms-and-induce-the-published-metrics]]) through the
defining supremum. The compatibility with matrix-vector multiplication, the
submultiplicativity and the value on identity matrices are
[[thm-induced-matrix-norms-are-compatible-submultiplicative-and-normalized]];
the explicit value at $p=1$ and the separate $\infty$-formula are
[[thm-induced-one-and-infinity-matrix-norms-are-max-column-and-row-sums]].

2. **Maximum row sum.** $\lVert A\rVert_\infty=\max_{i<m}\sum_{j<n}|a_{ij}|$.

Let $p\in\mathbb{Q}$ with $p\ge 1$ and let $m,n,q\in\mathbb{N}$, with the
induced $p$-norms of [[def-induced-matrix-p-norm]].

1. **Compatibility.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and every
   $x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $$\lVert Ax\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert x\rVert_p.$$
2. **Submultiplicativity.** For every $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb{R})$ and
   $B\in M_{n\times q}(\mathbb{R})$,
   $$\lVert AB\rVert_p\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_p\,\lVert B\rVert_p.$$

   $$\lVert I_n\rVert_p=1,$$

**Outputs.** Return $(p_0,0,0)$ when $\nu=0$ or $t=0$. Otherwise return `budget-exhausted` or `certificate-unavailable`, or an approximate vector $\widehat p$ and certified bounds $(T,E_{\rm alg})$ for which $\|p(t)-\widehat p\|_1\le T+E_{\rm alg}$. Here $T\ge mG_K(\mu)$ is an outward-certified Poisson-tail upper bound and $E_{\rm alg}$ bounds the arithmetic/algebraic error relative to the exact truncated accumulation. **Procedure.** For $\nu t>0$, set $m=\lceil\nu t\rceil$ and $\mu=\nu t/m$, so $0<\mu\le1$. A rounded backend must certify these values and inequalities; if it cannot, return `certificate-unavailable`. If $m>B$, return `budget-exhausted`. Set $K_{\max}=\lfloor B/m\rfloor-1$. $$G_K(\mu):=\frac{e^{-\mu}\mu^{K+1}}{(K+1)!\left(1-\mu/(K+2)\right)}\le\varepsilon/m.$$
